I'm picking **candidate 6**. I worked this out in my head, as the task required, without simulating it, so it's a judgement call and not a verified result.

- **Rejected for structural reasons:**
  - Candidate 1 has only 29 pairs instead of 30, so it is likely invalid.
  - Candidate 0 orders almost every day and pays the 56 fee about 28 times.
  - Candidate 5 orders only every three days, which means bigger batches and more holding cost for little saving.
  - Candidate 4 orders roughly the forecast itself. Real demand averages about 1.046 × forecast, so it will run short more often, and shortages are costly.
- **Why lean towards ordering more:** For product 0, each unit of unmet demand loses 13 (9 of margin plus a 4 penalty). An extra unit only costs 0.5 per day to hold, and unsold units carry over for up to 8 days. Product 1 is similar. So ordering a bit above the mean pays off.
- **Choosing among candidates 2, 3, 6 and 7:**
  - Candidate 7 orders about 1.29 × forecast. Because the plan doesn't react to stock levels, the surplus would build up and units would expire, costing 4 each.
  - Candidates 2 and 3 keep a smaller margin through to the end. Leftover stock at the end is worthless, so the last orders are partly wasted.
  - Candidate 6 orders more at the start, about 1.24 × forecast, then cuts back over the last orders (106/102/71 for product 0, 46/22 for product 1). That saves roughly 37 units of product 0 and 13 of product 1, which by my estimate is worth more than 200.
- **Main risk for candidate 6:** the order of 185 units of product 0 on day 16 arrives on day 18. Together with existing stock, it could go over the 236 limit, and the excess would be lost. Candidate 3 avoids this by splitting the order, but pays an extra 56 fee and doesn't cut back at the end. I judged the end cutback in candidate 6 to be worth more than that risk.

Я выбрал **кандидата 6**. Ниже оценка в уме по основным факторам, без симуляции.

- **Кандидат 1 не подходит.** В нём 29 пар, а нужно ровно 30.
- **Кандидат 0 проигрывает на постоянных расходах.** Он заказывает почти каждый день, и одна только плата 56 за день заказа съедает около 1 570. У планов с заказом раз в два дня эта плата около 730.
- **Кандидат 5 упирается во вместимость склада.** Крупные заказы раз в три дня держат на складе около трёх дней спроса по обоим товарам сразу. Запас подходит к пределу в 236 единиц, и часть прихода может пропасть.
- **Объём товара 0 лучше брать с запасом.** Каждая единица нехватки стоит 13: упущенные 9 маржи плюс неустойка 4. Лишняя единица стоит лишь 0,5 в день хранения и переходит на следующий день, поэтому более крупные заказы выгоднее, пока их вмещает склад. По этой причине кандидат 4 (около 1,04 от прогнозного спроса) хуже кандидатов 2, 3, 6 и 7 (около 1,2–1,35).
- **Кандидат 6 сокращает заказы к концу периода, а 7 и 2 — нет.** Кандидат 7 — это кандидат 2, увеличенный примерно на 13 % без сокращения в конце. Остатки после дня 29 ничего не стоят, так что лишние закупки в конце — чистая потеря. Кандидат 6 заказывает с запасом в начале и середине и уменьшает последние заказы обоих товаров.
- **Пик в день 18 (спрос около 113) он выдерживает почти без потерь.** Если считать по прогнозу, при приходе 185 единиц у кандидата 6 переполнение склада всего около 3 единиц. Кандидат 3 избегает переполнения, разбив заказ на два дня, но платит за это лишние 56. При этом в сам день 18 у него меньше товара под высокий спрос.

I picked candidate 6, but this is an estimate made in my head with no simulation, so treat it as a judgement call.

1. **Order frequency.** Ordering every other day looks best:
   - Daily orders (candidate 0) pay the 56 fixed fee about twice as often. The extra fees (~840) outweigh the storage saved (~660).
   - Ordering every third day (candidate 5) saves ~280 in fees. But the larger batches add roughly 20 a day in storage, about 660 over the month. Candidate 5 also risks going over the 236-unit limit around day 18.
   - Candidate 1 has only 29 pairs instead of 30, so I set it aside as invalid.
2. **Safety stock.** Running out costs far more than leftover stock does. A unit short of product 0 loses 9 of profit plus a 4 penalty, while a leftover unit costs about 1 in storage. Leftovers also stay sellable for 8 days and carry into the next order. So ordering well above the forecast pays off. Candidate 4 orders about the expected demand, which is too little. Candidates 2 and 3 order about 1.2× the forecast. Candidates 6 and 7 order about 1.25–1.3×, which is closer to the best level.
3. **End of the month.** Candidate 7 keeps ordering large amounts through day 26, so it is left holding unsold stock at the end, which is worth nothing. Candidate 6 cuts its last orders back to about expected demand (days 22–26).
4. **Capacity around day 18.** Candidate 6 may lose a few units to the storage limit when its 185 units of product 0 arrive on day 18. Candidate 3 avoids this by splitting that order. Lost units only cost their purchase price of about 4 each, though, so this matters less than candidate 6's higher safety stock.

Мой выбор — **кандидат 4**, но преимущество небольшое. Оценки сделаны в уме и приблизительно, без построчной симуляции.

1. **Количество заказов против числа заказов.** Стоимость заказа 56 сопоставима с затратами на хранение:
   - Ежедневный заказ (кандидаты 0 и 1) обходится примерно в 28 × 56 = 1568 платы за заказы.
   - Заказ раз в 2 дня (кандидаты 2, 3, 4, 6 и 7) — примерно в 14 × 56 = 784.
   - Цикл в 2 дня держит примерно на полдня спроса больше запаса. По хранению это около 21 в день, или примерно 580 за период. Поэтому цикл в 2 дня выгоднее ежедневного примерно на 200.
   - Цикл в 3 дня (кандидат 5) экономит только около 168 на заказах. Зато он добавляет ещё примерно 600 хранения и сильнее страдает от нехватки при колебаниях спроса.
2. **Объёмы внутри цикла в 2 дня.** Средний спрос примерно на 4,6 % выше прогноза.
   - Кандидат 4 заказывает почти ровно средний спрос: по товару 0 около 1240 единиц против ожидаемых примерно 1235. По товару 1 — около 673 против примерно 672.
   - Кандидаты 2 и 3 заказывают примерно на 14 % больше среднего, кандидаты 6 и 7 — ещё больше. Годность 8 дней, и продажи идут со старых партий, поэтому лишнее почти не списывается. Оно копится на складе.
   - У кандидатов 2 и 3 излишек товара 0 растёт до 150–170 единиц. Дополнительное хранение составляет около 750, плюс купленные единицы, которые в конце ничего не стоят. Сокращение нехватки возвращает лишь около 680.
   - По товару 1 запас выгоден ещё меньше: маржа у него всего 4, а хранение — 0,9.
3. **Переполнение склада.** Большой заказ на день 16 (185–190 единиц у кандидатов 2, 6 и 7) приходит в день 18. Вместе с остатками он рискует превысить 236 единиц, и излишек пропадёт. Кандидат 3 обходит это, разбивая заказ на два, но остаётся в целом перезаказанным.

**Риск:** кандидат 4 заказывает без запаса на колебания. Поэтому из-за случайности он потеряет примерно 50 единиц продаж товара 0. По моей оценке, это всё равно дешевле, чем хранить излишки у кандидатов 2, 3, 6 и 7.

Ближайший соперник — кандидат 0: он тоже заказывает примерно по среднему спросу, но каждый день. Мой перевес примерно в 200 в пользу кандидата 4 — порядок погрешности таких оценок.

I picked **Candidate 3**. I reasoned this out in my head and didn't simulate any plan, so this is a judgement call, not a computed result.

1. **Candidate 1 is out.** Its plan has 29 pairs instead of the required 30.
2. **Ordering every day costs too much.** Candidate 0 places an order nearly every day, which adds up to about 28 × 56 ≈ 1570 in fixed fees. Plans that order every other day pay that fee only about 13 times.
3. **Ordering every three days runs into problems.** Candidate 5's batches are large, so storage costs go up. The 236-unit warehouse limit could also cause stock to be lost.
4. **A small surplus is cheap, a shortage is expensive.** Each unit short costs about 13 for product 0 and about 7 for product 1. A leftover unit costs only 0.5 or 0.9 a day in storage. Goods keep for 8 days, so leftovers are sold in the next cycle. That makes it worth ordering somewhat above the forecast.
   - **Candidate 4** orders roughly at the forecast, which is too little.
   - **Candidates 2 and 3** order about 14% above the expected demand (forecast × 1.046), which is a reasonable margin.
   - **Candidates 6 and 7** order more still.
5. **The demand spike around day 18 decides it.** On days 18–19 the forecast for product 0 is 113 + 51.
   - Candidates 2, 6 and 7 cover this with a single delivery of 185–190 units on day 18. Together with the product 1 stock and leftover product 0, the warehouse probably goes over 236, and the extra units are lost.
   - Candidate 3 splits the order into 136 on day 16 and 61 on day 17, so the goods arrive on days 18 and 19 and fit within capacity.
   - Apart from this split, Candidates 2 and 3 are identical, so Candidate 3 is ahead of Candidate 2 and is the best overall.

I pick **candidate 4**, with moderate confidence. Everything below is a rough mental estimate, as the task required.

**Disqualified**
- **Candidate 1** has only 29 pairs instead of 30, so the plan is invalid.

**Ordering every 2 days beats ordering daily or every 3 days**
- **Candidate 0** orders every day, which is 28 order days and about 1,568 in fixed fees. Plans that order every 2 days have 13 order days and pay about 728. Smaller daily batches save only about 650 in storage, so candidate 0 ends up roughly 200 behind.
- **Candidate 5** orders every 3 days. It has 11 order days, saving only about 112 in fees, but it carries about one extra day of stock. That costs roughly 620 more in storage. Some days it also runs close to the 236-unit capacity.

**Comparing the every-2-days plans (2, 3, 4, 6, 7) by how much they order against expected demand**
Expected demand is the forecast × 1.046.
- **Candidate 4** is almost exactly balanced:
  - Item 0: about 1,240 ordered against about 1,235 expected demand from day 2 on.
  - Item 1: about 673 ordered against about 672 expected demand from day 5 on.
- **Candidate 2** orders about 170 extra of item 0 and about 68 extra of item 1. Shelf life is 8 days and the oldest stock sells first, so the surplus doesn't expire. It piles up instead: on average about 85 units of item 0 are kept for about 28 days, which costs about 1,100 in storage. The stock left at the end is worthless, which loses about 680 in purchase cost. Later in the month the stock pile also reaches the 236-unit capacity, so arriving deliveries spill over and are lost.
- **Candidate 4's** shortages: with a balanced plan, the stock level drifts randomly up and down. I estimate about 60–65 units of item 0 go unsold over the month, costing about 13 each in lost margin plus penalty, so about 850. That is still about 400 better than candidate 2 for item 0. Item 1 has a small margin, so candidate 2's surplus there costs more than the shortages it prevents.
- **Candidate 3** is the same as 2, except it pays an extra 56 to split the day-16 order. That saves only about 30 in storage, so it is slightly worse than 2.
- **Candidates 6 and 7** order 30–35% more than the forecast. They pile up even more stock, pay more storage and run into the capacity limit harder, so they are the worst of this group.

**Uncertainty:** candidate 4 does run short more often in low-stock periods. Still, overstocking costs the other plans a lot more on average.

I picked **candidate 4**: it orders every other day and buys about as much as average demand. I checked this with rough arithmetic only, not a full day-by-day trace. Candidates 0 and 4 are fairly close; the rest fall further behind.

**1. How often to order (each day with an order costs 56)**
- **Candidates 0 and 1 order every day:** 28 days × 56 = 1568. Ordering every other day costs 14 × 56 = 784. The extra stock that every-other-day ordering holds overnight costs about 22 per day in storage, roughly 616 over the month. Every other day still comes out about 170 ahead.
- **Candidate 5 orders every third day:** 11 × 56 = 616. That saves only about 168 in ordering fees but adds roughly another 616 in storage. On days 5 and 8, deliveries of both products total about 200 units at once, close to the 236-unit limit. Candidate 5 is worse.

**2. How much to order (candidates 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 all order every other day)**
These plans are fixed in advance and don't react to actual sales. Any surplus therefore carries over and builds up. You pay storage on it every day, and whatever is left at the end is lost. Lost sales, on the other hand, partly even out between periods.
- **Product 0:** average demand for days 2–29 is 1181 × 1.046 ≈ 1235. Candidate 4 orders 1240, almost exactly that. Candidate 2 orders 1405, about 170 too many. That surplus costs roughly 1000 or more in storage plus about 680 in purchase cost, which outweighs the shortage penalties it avoids.
- **Product 1:** average demand for days 5–29 is 642 × 1.046 ≈ 672. Candidate 4 orders 673. Candidate 2 orders 740, and each extra unit costs 7 to buy plus 0.9 per day to store.
- **Candidates 6 and 7** order even more than candidate 2, so they lose more. **Candidate 3** is candidate 2 with the day-16 order split in two: it costs an extra 56 and adds more surplus.

**3. Effect of random demand**
Candidate 4 keeps no extra buffer, so the random swings will cause some lost sales of product 0, roughly 450 in total. That is still less than what over-ordering costs. Product 1 runs short on days 0–4 in every plan: its first delivery can't arrive before day 5.

I picked **candidate 2**. This is a mental estimate, not a simulation: nothing was run, as the task required.

Leftover stock doesn't spoil quickly (it keeps 8 days), so the cost of ordering too much is mostly storage. That favours ordering about 1.2 × the two-day forecast. I chose **candidate 4**, but this rests on a rough mental estimate, not a simulation. Candidates 2 and 6 are close behind.

- **Candidate 1 is out**: it has only 29 order pairs, and the task requires exactly 30.
- **Ordering every day costs too much (candidate 0)**: it pays the 56 fee about 25 times, against about 14 for the every-other-day plans. That is roughly 600 extra, with no advantage on margin to make it back.

  - Candidate 4 orders about 1240 for that period, almost exactly the expected demand.
  - Candidate 2 orders about 1405, roughly 170 more.
  - Candidate 6 orders about 1443, roughly 208 more.
- **That surplus is expensive**: by around day 23, candidate 2 is carrying about 130 extra units of product 0 and candidate 6 about 205. At 0.5 per unit per day over about 20 days, that is roughly 1,300 or more. Anything still unsold at the end is a lost 4 per unit.
- **Candidate 4's risk is running short**: each missing unit of product 0 costs 13 (9 lost margin plus a penalty of 4). By my rough estimate that comes to about 900 over the run, less than the holding cost the bigger plans pay.
- **Candidates 3, 5 and 7**: candidate 7 orders even more than 6. Candidates 3 and 5 split or merge orders without fixing the surplus problem.

**Answer: candidate 3**, but only just. My estimate puts it barely ahead of candidate 2, and the gap between them is within the noise. Both look clearly better than the other six. I did the arithmetic in my head on forecast values.

**Plans that order every day (0 and 1).** The fixed fee comes to about 28 × 56 ≈ 1570. Ordering every other day cuts the fee to about 730 and costs only about 0.5 of a day's demand in extra stock. That works out to roughly 20 per day in storage, or about 650 over the month. So ordering every other day saves about 200 overall. Candidate 0 also orders about the forecast itself, which is below the true average demand (multiplier average 1.046). That means frequent shortages, at 13 per unit for good 0.

**Plan that orders every 3 days (5).** It saves only about 170 in fees compared with every other day. It holds about 0.5 of a day's demand more stock of both goods, which costs about 22 per day, or roughly 650 over the month. It also brings the warehouse close to its 236-unit limit on delivery days, so some delivered stock can be lost.

**Every-other-day plans: how much to order.** Good 0 has an expensive shortage (13 per unit) and a cheap surplus, because leftovers keep for 8 days at 0.5 per day. Good 1 has shortage and spoilage costs that are both about 7. So the right order is a little above true demand: about 1.1–1.2 × forecast for good 0 and about 1.05–1.1 × forecast for good 1.
- Candidate 4 orders about 1.045 × forecast, which is just the true average. With no safety margin, it runs short of good 0.
- Candidates 6 and 7 order about 1.3 × forecast. Surplus builds up and spoils. They also put 185–190 units of good 0 into the warehouse on day 18, which overflows it.
- Candidates 2 and 3 order about 1.19 × forecast for good 0 and 1.14 × forecast for good 1. This is the best fit.

**Candidate 2 vs candidate 3.** The only difference is day 16. On the morning of day 18 I estimate about 70 units already in the warehouse (about 25 of good 0 and about 45 of good 1). Candidate 2's delivery of 185 would then lose about 19 units to overflow. Candidate 3 splits the order into 136 + 61 across days 18 and 19. That avoids the overflow and covers more of the demand spike (forecast 113 on day 18). It costs an extra 56 order fee plus 12 more units. I estimate the gain from fewer shortages and less overflow at about +100 and the extra cost at about −104, so it's a near tie. I pick 3 because it also stores a bit less on the evening of day 18 and holds up better if demand that day comes in high.

I picked **candidate 6**. I worked this out by estimation, not a full day-by-day simulation, so it is a best guess.

- **Ruled out first:** candidate 1 has only 29 pairs, so it isn't a valid plan. Candidates 0 and 1 also order every day, which costs about 28 × 56 ≈ 1570 in fees. Plans that order every other day pay about half of that.

Over-ordering is cheap because unsold stock carries over (only storage of 0.5 or 0.9 per day until it expires). So it pays to order well above the forecast. Candidate 6 orders about 1.3× the forecast. Candidates 2 and 3 order about 1.2× and candidate 4 about 1.05×, which risks more shortage penalties.
- **Why not candidate 7:** it orders even more (about 1.34×). Around day 18, when the order of 190 units of product 0 arrives, total stock would come to about 255 against the 236-unit limit, so the excess would be lost. Candidate 6 sits right at the limit there, about 240.
- **End of the month:** candidate 6 orders less near the end (106, 102, 71 for product 0; 22 for product 1 on day 24), which leaves fewer worthless units at day 29. Candidates 2 and 7 keep ordering heavily to the end.

I estimated this roughly in my head rather than simulating it. My pick is **candidate 6**, but candidates 2, 3 and 7 are close enough that the ranking could change.
